name: AI in Education
blurb: Artificial intelligence is already in schools, in the tools teachers plan with, the software students practise on, and the systems that run buses and budgets. These pages, built on the book The AI Ready School, set out what works from preschool to graduation, what the evidence shows, and the rule that runs through all of it: AI may inform a decision about a child, but a named person makes it.

children.name: Getting Oriented
children.blurb: The first four chapters lay the foundation for everything that follows. They explain what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool.

children.name: The Classroom
children.blurb: Part II, The Classroom, covers AI in each stage and subject. It begins with preschool through second grade, then turns to reading and writing, mathematics, science and computing, social studies and world languages, the arts and physical education, and personalized learning and tutoring.

children.name: Every Student, Every Family
children.blurb: Part III, Every Student, Every Family, covers special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. These chapters address the students and families who most need careful attention.

children.name: Running the School
children.blurb: Part IV, Running the School, covers teacher planning and grading, assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership. These chapters speak most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members.

sections.body: This part of school life is the use of AI in education, where schools are responsible not only for running operations but also for how AI affects children's learning and safety. The book gathers 300 practical ideas across 20 chapters, from preschool through graduation and from the classroom to the business office, each with an evidence label. It describes students finding free chat tools before policies existed, teachers using AI to plan lessons before training, vendors adding AI to products schools already owned, and leaders facing choices about tools they had never evaluated. It shows the same kind of tool producing opposite results: a plain chatbot in Turkey led many students to copy answers and score worse later, while a tool designed and supervised by teachers in Nigeria produced gains. It also points to family messages and counselor reminders that improved attendance and grades and helped students reach college, and it treats AI as something that can help learning or block it depending on adult choices.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI tutoring works when teachers design the opening prompt, stay in the room, and keep the tool giving hints rather than answers. It finds that plain chatbots used alone can harm learning, that AI detectors misclassify writing by students still learning English, and that no evidence shows online monitoring prevents harm. It also reports no independent evaluation of AI security systems in schools and says research on young children and students with disabilities is thin. The rules it holds to are that people make every decision affecting a student, names and details stay out of tools without a signed data privacy agreement, every AI draft is checked by a person, and every flag leads to a person who reaches out. It adds that adoption succeeds when leaders model use, measure hours saved and student outcomes, and publish rules for privacy, review, and accountability, because tools do not change schools and the people in them do.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a path from orientation to daily practice, family partnership, and school operations. Getting Oriented gives the reader the book's purpose, its explanation of AI in plain language, its evidence labels, its five rules, and its honesty about what is not yet known. The Classroom is where a teacher would go for practical ideas on planning, teaching, feedback, and grading, organized by subject and grade. Every Student, Every Family is where a parent would go to understand how children use AI, whether the school protects them, and what questions to ask a school, while also covering messages and reminders that reach families. Running the School is where a principal, district leader, or board member would go for policy, pilots, purchasing, professional learning, the questions a board should ask, and the first 90 days for leaders, teachers, and parents.
